claims.text: Silicon pack cementation at 1100–1200 °C under an inert or slightly reducing atmosphere will produce controlled silicon enrichment at the ZrB2 surface without deep penetration.
The treatment will form a thin, uniform silicon-enriched surface layer on ZrB2.
The introduced silicon will diffuse into the surface region of ZrB2.
Silicon in the modified surface will react to form zirconium-silicide phases.
The modified surface will form borosilicate compounds.
The resulting silicide/borosilicate layer will be chemically inert toward molten aluminum.
The resulting silicide/borosilicate layer will have low aluminum solubility.
The silicide/borosilicate layer will act as a diffusion barrier that limits molten-aluminum penetration.
Limiting aluminum penetration will retard the reactive-diffusion processes responsible for corrosion of ZrB2.
Silicon-pack-cemented ZrB2 will have a significantly lower molten-aluminum corrosion rate than untreated ZrB2.
Treated ZrB2 will exhibit less mass loss than untreated ZrB2 during molten-aluminum immersion.
Treated ZrB2 will exhibit a shallower aluminum penetration depth than untreated ZrB2 during molten-aluminum immersion.
The protective layer should remain effective at approximately 660 °C for exposure durations relevant to industrial hot-dip aluminum-plating cycles.
Excessive silicon penetration or formation of an overly thick modified layer may degrade the barrier properties.
Excessive silicon penetration or formation of an overly thick modified layer may compromise the mechanical integrity of the ZrB2 component.
A controlled inert or slightly reducing atmosphere during treatment will prevent unwanted oxidation.

contradictions.description: The treatment atmosphere is specified to prevent oxidation, yet borosilicate formation is proposed during surface modification without identifying an oxygen source or a later oxidation step. The timing and conditions for forming the oxygen-containing borosilicate phase are therefore internally unresolved.
